e.t: This word is a proper place name, referring to Beth-car, a location mentioned in 1 Samuel 7:11. “Beth” functions as part of that place name rather than as an ordinary action, quality, or description. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in the same verse. The surrounding verse identifies how the name functions in that passage, while the word itself primarily serves to identify the location.

This Hebrew word means “old.” It functions as a describing word, identifying a person, thing, or condition as old. Its sense is used across the Old Testament rather than being limited to one setting, appearing 16 times in 15 verses. The surrounding noun or sentence determines exactly what is being described, so the word may refer to age or an old condition without changing its central meaning. It occurs from Genesis through Lamentations, showing continued use across the Hebrew Scriptures.

This Hebrew noun means “shekel,” referring to a measured unit of value or weight. It appears twice in the Old Testament, in Genesis and Exodus, and is associated with counted or given amounts. The word can occur in expressions describing a portion of a shekel, so its precise numerical value comes from the surrounding passage rather than from the noun alone. Its basic sense remains a shekel as a recognized unit used in biblical accounting.

This Hebrew word means “out.” It functions as a predicate, expressing an action or state associated with what is being discussed rather than naming a person, place, or thing. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Psalm 71:6. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that sentence depends on the context. Its basic contribution is the idea of being or coming “out.”

e.t: Gera is a personal name, rendered “Gera.” It identifies an individual in the Hebrew Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or object. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but its ordinary function is simply to name a person. This name is found in Genesis, Judges, Samuel, Kings, and Chronicles.

This Hebrew word expresses being “afraid” and can describe something “dreadful.” Its use may refer to the fear people experience or to something that inspires fear. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs six times, all in Daniel, where it is used for frightening appearances and for fear connected with the authority of God and rulers. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

e.h: A Hebrew Word for That One
e.t: This Hebrew word points to a particular person or thing, with the sense of identifying “that one” or “the one being indicated.” It functions as a demonstrative expression rather than naming an action, quality, or relationship. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Genesis: Genesis 24:65 and Genesis 37:19. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic role is to direct attention to a specific referent.

Horam is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Horam.” It identifies one individual rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this name appears once, in Joshua 10:33. Because no descriptive definition is provided for the name, its significance here is its role in identifying the person mentioned, not a separate lexical idea such as a virtue, command, or event.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “strength.” It refers to the ability, capacity, or force by which someone or something acts, endures, or accomplishes what is needed. Its exact force depends on the sentence, but the central idea remains strength as effective capacity. This word occurs 127 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing that it is used broadly for strength and power in many settings.

This Hebrew word means “atonement,” referring to the appointed means by which wrongdoing is dealt with before God. In the Old Testament, it is used seven times, especially in passages about sacrifices, the altar, appointed holy days, and restoring what has been wrongfully taken. The word therefore points to atonement as a recognized act within worship and reconciliation, rather than merely a private feeling of regret. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Likhi is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Likhi.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 7:19. Because it is a name, its meaning is not explained by translating it into an ordinary English concept; its function is to identify the individual named in that genealogy.

Middin is a proper place name, referring to a location called “Middin.” It is not presented here as an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 15:61, and the English renderings preserve it as “Middin.” Without the surrounding verse text, no further contextual meaning should be assigned to the name. Its significance is therefore chiefly geographic: it identifies one place among the locations named in that passage.

The repeated use of “coupling” presents the word as a practical term for joining components into one connected arrangement.

Its exact significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and boundary description.
